segs.e: Linked Discourses 10.1
1. With Indaka
With Indaka
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati indakūṭe pabbate, indakassa yakkhassa bhavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha on Mount Indra’s Peak, the haunt of the native spirit Indaka.

segs.p: Atha kho indako yakkho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: Then the native spirit Indaka went up to the Buddha, and addressed him in verse:
“The Buddhas say that form is not the soul.
Then how does this one obtain this body?
From where do his bones and organs come?
How does this one coalesce in the womb?”
“First there’s the zygote;
then there’s the blastocyst;
from there arises the gastrula;
which produces the embryonic mass.
From that the limb buds appear,
the head hair, body hair, and nails.
And whatever the mother eats—
the food and drink that she consumes—
nourishes them there,
the person in the mother’s womb.”
Linked Discourses 10.2
1. With Indaka
Sakka In Name Only

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

segs.p: Atha kho sakkanāmako yakkho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: Then a spirit who was Sakka in name only went up to the Buddha, and addressed him in verse:
“You’ve given up all ties,
and are fully freed.
It’s not a good idea for you, ascetic,
to be instructing others.”
“No matter how you explain why
people gather together, Sakka,
it’s unworthy for a wise person
not to think of the other with sympathy.
If you instruct others
with a mind clear and confident,
your compassion and empathy
don’t create attachments.”
Linked Discourses 10.3
1. With Indaka
With Spiky

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā gayāyaṁ viharati ṭaṅkitamañce sūcilomassa yakkhassa bhavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Gayā on the cut-stone ledge in the haunt of Spiky the native spirit.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena kharo ca yakkho sūcilomo ca yakkho bhagavato avidūre atikkamanti.
segs.e: Now at that time the native spirits Shaggy and Spiky were passing by not far from the Buddha.

segs.p: Atha kho kharo yakkho sūcilomaṁ yakkhaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: So Shaggy said to Spiky,
“That’s an ascetic.”
“That’s no ascetic, he’s a faker!

segs.p: Yāva jānāmi yadi vā so samaṇo yadi vā pana so samaṇako”ti.
segs.e: I’ll soon find out whether he’s an ascetic or a faker.”

segs.p: Atha kho sūcilomo yakkho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato kāyaṁ upanāmesi.
segs.e: Then Spiky went up to the Buddha and leaned up against his body,
but the Buddha pulled away.

segs.p: Atha kho sūcilomo yakkho bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Spiky said to the Buddha,
“Are you afraid, ascetic?”
“No, respectable sir, I’m not afraid.
But your touch is nasty.”
“I will ask you a question, ascetic.

segs.p: Sace me na byākarissasi, cittaṁ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṁ vā te phālessāmi, pādesu vā gahetvā pāragaṅgāya khipissāmī”ti.
segs.e: If you don’t answer me, I’ll drive you insane, or explode your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you to the far shore of the Ganges!”

segs.p: “Na khvāhaṁ taṁ, āvuso, passāmi sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya, yo me cittaṁ vā khipeyya hadayaṁ vā phāleyya pādesu vā gahetvā pāragaṅgāya khipeyya;
segs.e: “I don’t see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans who could do that to me.

segs.p: api ca tvaṁ, āvuso, puccha yadā kaṅkhasī”ti. (…)
segs.e: But anyway, ask what you wish.”
“Where do greed and hate come from?
From where spring discontent, desire, and terror?
Where do the mind’s thoughts originate,
like a crow let loose by boys.”
“Greed and hate come from here;
from here spring discontent, desire, and terror;
here’s where the mind’s thoughts originate,
like a crow let loose by boys.
Born of affection, originating in oneself,
like prop roots sprouting from a banyan;
the many kinds of attachment to sensual pleasures
are like camel’s foot creeper <j>creeping through the woods.
Those who understand where they come from
dispel them—listen up, spirit!
They cross this flood so hard to cross,
not crossed before, so as to not be reborn.”
Linked Discourses 10.4
1. With Indaka
With Maṇibhadda

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā magadhesu viharati maṇimālike cetiye maṇibhaddassa yakkhassa bhavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Magadhans at the Maṇimālika Shrine, the haunt of the native spirit Maṇibhadda.

segs.p: Atha kho maṇibhaddo yakkho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato santike imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Then the native spirit Maṇibhadda went up to the Buddha, and spoke this verse in the Buddha’s presence:
“It’s always auspicious for the mindful;
the mindful prosper in happiness.
Each new day is better for the mindful,
and they are freed from enmity.”
“It’s always auspicious for the mindful;
the mindful prosper in happiness.
Each new day is better for the mindful,
but they’re not freed from enmity.
But someone whose mind delights in harmlessness,
all day and all night,
with love for all living creatures—
they have no enmity for anyone.”
Linked Discourses 10.5
1. With Indaka
With Sānu

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññatarissā upāsikāya sānu nāma putto yakkhena gahito hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time a certain lay woman had a son named Sānu who had been seized by a native spirit.

segs.p: Atha kho sā upāsikā paridevamānā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: And as that lay woman wept, on that occasion she recited these verses:
“I have heard this from the perfected ones.
The native spirits will not mess with anyone
who leads the spiritual life
by observing the sabbath
complete in all eight factors
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnight of special displays.
But now today I see
native spirits messing with Sānu.”
“What you heard from the perfected ones is right.
The native spirits will not mess with anyone
who leads the spiritual life
by observing the sabbath
complete in all eight factors
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnight of special displays.
When Sānu regains consciousness tell him
this saying of the native spirits:
Don’t do bad deeds
either openly or in secret.
If you should do a bad deed,
or you’re doing one now,
you won’t be freed from suffering,
though you fly away and flee.”
“Mum, they cry for the dead,
or for one who’s alive but missing.
I’m alive and you can see me,
so mum, why do you weep for me?”
“Son, they cry for the dead,
or for one who’s alive but missing.
But someone who has given up sensual pleasures
only to come back here again:
they cry for them as well,
for though still alive they’re really dead.
My dear, you’ve been rescued from hot coals,
and you want to plunge right back in them!
My dear, you’ve been rescued from the abyss,
and you want to plunge right back there!
Hurry up, good luck to you!
To whom should we complain?
A valuable saved from a fire,
you want to burn again!”
Linked Discourses 10.6
1. With Indaka
With Piyaṅkara

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ āyasmā anuruddho sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā anuruddho rattiyā paccūsasamayaṁ paccuṭṭhāya dhammapadāni bhāsati.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Anuruddha rose at the crack of dawn and recited passages of the teaching.

segs.p: Atha kho piyaṅkaramātā yakkhinī puttakaṁ evaṁ tosesi:
segs.e: Then the native spirit Piyaṅkara’s Mother soothed her little child, saying:
“Don’t make a sound, Piyaṅkara!
A mendicant recites passages of the teaching.
When we understand a passage,
we can practice for our welfare.
Let us restrain ourselves from harming living creatures,
and speak no lying words.
We should train ourselves well in ethics,
and hopefully we’ll be freed from the goblin realm.”
Linked Discourses 10.7
1. With Indaka
With Punabbasu

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā bhikkhū nibbānapaṭisaṁyuttāya dhammiyā kathāya sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṁseti.
segs.e: Now at that time the Buddha was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants with a Dhamma talk about extinguishment.

segs.p: Te ca bhikkhū aṭṭhiṁ katvā manasi katvā sabbacetasā samannāharitvā ohitasotā dhammaṁ suṇanti.
segs.e: And those mendicants were paying attention, applying the mind, concentrating wholeheartedly, and actively listening.

segs.p: Atha kho punabbasumātā yakkhinī puttake evaṁ tosesi:
segs.e: Then the native spirit Punabbasu’s Mother soothed her little children, saying:
“Hush, little Uttarā!
Hush, Punabbasu!
For I want to listen to the teaching
of the Teacher, the supreme Buddha.
Extinguishment, the Blessed One said,
is the release from all ties.
I have a lasting love
for this teaching.
In this world, your own child is dear;
in this world, your own husband is dear;
but even greater than that is my love
for this teaching’s quest.
For neither son nor husband,
dear as they are, can free you from suffering;
as listening to the true teaching
frees living creatures from suffering.
In this world mired in suffering,
fettered by old age and death,
I want to listen to the teaching
through which the Buddha awakened,
which frees you from old age and death.
So hush, Punabbasu!”
“Mom, I’m not speaking,
and Uttarā is silent, too.
Focus just on the teaching,
for it’s nice to listen to the true teaching.
And it’s because we haven’t understood the teaching
that we live in suffering, Mom.
He is a beacon for those who are lost
among gods and humans.
The Buddha, bearing his final body,
the Clear-eyed One teaches Dhamma.”
“It’s good that my child’s so astute,
this child I bore and suckled!
My child loves the pure teaching
of the supreme Buddha.
Punabbasu, may you be happy!
Today, I rise.
Hear me too, Uttarā:
I have seen the noble truths!”
Linked Discourses 10.8
1. With Indaka
With Sudatta

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati sītavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Cool Grove.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati rājagahaṁ anuppatto hoti kenacideva karaṇīyena.
segs.e: Now at that time the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had arrived at Rājagaha on some business.
He heard
a rumor that a Buddha had arisen in the world.

segs.p: Tāvadeva ca pana bhagavantaṁ dassanāya upasaṅkamitukāmo hoti. Athassa anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa etadahosi:
segs.e: Right away he wanted to go and see the Buddha, but he thought,
“It’s too late to go and see the Buddha today.

segs.p: Sve dānāhaṁ kālena bhagavantaṁ dassanāya gamissāmī”ti buddhagatāya satiyā nipajji.
segs.e: I’ll go and see him tomorrow.” He went to bed thinking of the Buddha.

segs.p: Rattiyā sudaṁ tikkhattuṁ vuṭṭhāsi pabhātanti maññamāno.
segs.e: During the night he got up three times thinking it was sunup.

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati yena sivathikadvāraṁ tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then he approached the Sivaka Gate,
and non-human beings opened it for him.

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa nagaramhā nikkhamantassa āloko antaradhāyi, andhakāro pāturahosi, bhayaṁ chambhitattaṁ lomahaṁso udapādi, tatova puna nivattitukāmo ahosi.
segs.e: But as he was leaving the city, light vanished and darkness appeared to him. He felt fear, terror, and goosebumps, and wanted to turn back.

segs.p: Atha kho sivako yakkho antarahito saddamanussāvesi:
segs.e: Then the invisible spirit Sivaka called out:
“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses,
a hundred mule-drawn chariots,
a hundred thousand maidens
bedecked with jeweled earrings:
these are not worth a sixteenth part
of a single forward stride!
Forward, householder!
Forward, householder!
Going forward is better for you,
not turning back!”

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa andhakāro antaradhāyi, āloko pāturahosi, yaṁ ahosi bhayaṁ chambhitattaṁ lomahaṁso, so paṭippassambhi.
segs.e: Then darkness vanished and light appeared to Anāthapiṇḍika. His fear, terror, and goosebumps settled down.

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa āloko antaradhāyi, andhakāro pāturahosi, bhayaṁ chambhitattaṁ lomahaṁso udapādi, tatova puna nivattitukāmo ahosi.
segs.e: But for a second time, light vanished and darkness appeared to him. …

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho sivako yakkho antarahito saddamanussāvesi:
segs.e: For a second time the invisible spirit Sivaka called out …
“… Going forward is better for you,
not turning back!”

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa andhakāro antaradhāyi, āloko pāturahosi, yaṁ ahosi bhayaṁ chambhitattaṁ lomahaṁso, so paṭippassambhi.
segs.e: Then darkness vanished and light appeared to Anāthapiṇḍika. His fear, terror, and goosebumps settled down.

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa āloko antaradhāyi, andhakāro pāturahosi, bhayaṁ chambhitattaṁ lomahaṁso udapādi, tatova puna nivattitukāmo ahosi.
segs.e: But for a third time, light vanished and darkness appeared to him. …

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho sivako yakkho antarahito saddamanussāvesi:
segs.e: For a third time the invisible spirit Sivaka called out …
“… Going forward is better for you,
not turning back!”

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa andhakāro antaradhāyi, āloko pāturahosi, yaṁ ahosi bhayaṁ chambhitattaṁ lomahaṁso, so paṭippassambhi.
segs.e: Then darkness vanished and light appeared to Anāthapiṇḍika. His fear, terror, and goosebumps settled down.

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati yena sītavanaṁ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to the Cool Grove and approached the Buddha.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā rattiyā paccūsasamayaṁ paccuṭṭhāya abbhokāse caṅkamati.
segs.e: Now at that time the Buddha had risen at the crack of dawn and was walking mindfully in the open.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā anāthapiṇḍikaṁ gahapatiṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: He saw Anāthapiṇḍika coming off in the distance.

segs.p: Disvāna caṅkamā orohitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: So he stepped down from the walking path, sat down on the seat spread out,

segs.p: Nisajja kho bhagavā anāthapiṇḍikaṁ gahapatiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: and said to Anāthapiṇḍika,
“Come, Sudatta.”

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati, nāmena maṁ bhagavā ālapatīti, haṭṭho udaggo tattheva bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Anāthapiṇḍika thought, “The Buddha calls me by name!” Smiling and elated, he bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet and said to him,
“Sir, I trust the Buddha slept well?”
“A brahmin who is fully quenched
always sleeps at ease.
Sensual pleasures slip off them,
they’re cooled, free of attachments.
Since they’ve cut off all clinging,
and removed the stress from the heart,
the peaceful sleep at ease,
having found peace of mind.”
Linked Discourses 10.9
1. With Indaka
With the Nun Sukkā (1st)

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena sukkā bhikkhunī mahatiyā parisāya parivutā dhammaṁ deseti.
segs.e: Now, at that time the nun Sukkā was teaching Dhamma, surrounded by a large assembly.

segs.p: Atha kho sukkāya bhikkhuniyā abhippasanno yakkho rājagahe rathikāya rathikaṁ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṁ upasaṅkamitvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imā gāthāyo abhāsi:
segs.e: Then a native spirit was so devoted to Sukkā that he went from street to street and from square to square, and on that occasion recited these verses:
“What’s up with these people in Rājagaha?
They sleep like they’ve been drinking mead!
They don’t attend on Sukkā
as she’s teaching the state free of death.
But the wise—
it’s as if they drink it up,
so irresistible, delectable, and nutritious,
like travelers enjoying a cool cloud.”
Linked Discourses 10.10
1. With Indaka
With the Nun Sukkā (2nd)

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññataro upāsako sukkāya bhikkhuniyā bhojanaṁ adāsi.
segs.e: Now at that time a certain lay follower gave food to the nun Sukkā.

segs.p: Atha kho sukkāya bhikkhuniyā abhippasanno yakkho rājagahe rathikāya rathikaṁ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṁ upasaṅkamitvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Then a native spirit was so devoted to Sukkā that he went from street to street and from square to square, and on that occasion recited these verses:
“O! He has made so much merit!
That lay follower is so very wise.
He just gave food to Sukkā,
who is released from all ties.”
Linked Discourses 10.11
1. With Indaka
With the Nun Cīrā
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññataro upāsako cīrāya bhikkhuniyā cīvaraṁ adāsi.
segs.e: Now at that time a certain lay follower gave a robe to the nun Cīrā.

segs.p: Atha kho cīrāya bhikkhuniyā abhippasanno yakkho rājagahe rathikāya rathikaṁ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṁ upasaṅkamitvā tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Then a native spirit was so devoted to Cīrā that he went from street to street and from square to square, and on that occasion recited these verses:
“O! He has made so much merit!
That lay-follower is so very wise.
He gave a robe to Cīrā,
who is released from all yokes.”
Linked Discourses 10.12
1. With Indaka
With Āḷavaka
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā āḷaviyaṁ viharati āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī in the haunt of the native spirit Āḷavaka.

segs.p: Atha kho āḷavako yakkho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the native spirit Āḷavaka went up to the Buddha, and said to him:
“Get out, ascetic!”
Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went out.
“Get in, ascetic!”
Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went in.

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho āḷavako yakkho bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And for a second time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha,
“Get out, ascetic!”
Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went out.
“Get in, ascetic!”
Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went in.

segs.p: Tatiyampi kho āḷavako yakkho bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And for a third time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha,
“Get out, ascetic!”
Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went out.
“Get in, ascetic!”
Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went in.

segs.p: Catutthampi kho āḷavako yakkho bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And for a fourth time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha,
“Get out, ascetic!”
“No, respectable sir, I won’t get out.
Do what you must.”
“I will ask you a question, ascetic.

segs.p: Sace me na byākarissasi, cittaṁ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṁ vā te phālessāmi, pādesu vā gahetvā pāragaṅgāya khipissāmī”ti.
segs.e: If you don’t answer me, I’ll drive you insane, or explode your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you to the far shore of the Ganges!”

segs.p: “Na khvāhaṁ taṁ, āvuso, passāmi sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya, yo me cittaṁ vā khipeyya hadayaṁ vā phāleyya, pādesu vā gahetvā pāragaṅgāya khipeyya.
segs.e: “I don’t see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans who could do that to me.

segs.p: Api ca tvaṁ, āvuso, puccha yadā kaṅkhasī”ti (…).
segs.e: But anyway, ask what you wish.”
“What’s a person’s best wealth?
What brings happiness when practiced well?
What’s the sweetest taste of all?
The one they say has the best life: how do they live?”
“Faith here is a person’s best wealth.
The teaching brings happiness when practiced well.
Truth is the sweetest taste of all.
The one they say has the best life lives by wisdom.”
“How do you cross the flood?
How do you cross the deluge?
How do you get over suffering?
How do you get purified?”
“By faith you cross the flood,
and by diligence the deluge.
By energy you get past suffering,
and you’re purified by wisdom.”
“How do you get wisdom?
How do you earn wealth?
How do you get a good reputation?
How do you hold on to friends?
How do the departed not grieve
when passing from this world to the next?”
“One who is diligent and discerning
gains wisdom by wanting to learn,
having faith in the perfected ones,
and the teaching for becoming extinguished.
Being responsible, acting appropriately,
and working hard you earn wealth.
Truthfulness wins you a good reputation.
You hold on to friends by giving.
That’s how the departed do not grieve
when passing from this world to the next.
A faithful householder of discernment
who possesses these four qualities
does not grieve after passing away:
truth, principle, steadfastness, and generosity.
Go ahead, ask others as well,
there are many ascetics and brahmins.
See whether anything better is found
than truth, principle, generosity, and patience.”
“Why now would I question
the many ascetics and brahmins?
Today I understand
what’s good for lives to come.
It was truly for my benefit
that the Buddha came to stay at Āḷavī.
Today I understand
where a gift is very fruitful.
I myself will journey
village to village, town to town,
paying homage to the Buddha,
and the clear rightness of the teaching!”
The Linked Discourses with Native Spirits are complete.
